planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet soil in partial to full shade, ideally in a container or pond-margin planter with a barrier; dwarf horsetail spreads by rhizome and, like all Equisetum, can become difficult to control if planted directly in garden soil.

Equisetum scirpoides is a diminutive, wiry, evergreen relative of the larger common horsetail, forming a low tangle of thread-thin, curling, dark green segmented stems that give it a fine, almost mossy texture quite different from its taller, coarser relatives. Its small scale and tolerance of constant moisture and shade make it useful in a bog garden, container water feature, or the shaded edge of a pond where its curling stems provide unusual year-round textural interest. Confine it firmly, since even the dwarf species spreads steadily by rhizome, and it will colonize any consistently damp soil it can reach.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Pleniflora' suckers more vigorously than single-flowered kerria and is best given room to form a naturalized colony or planted where suckers can be mowed or pulled to control spread.

This double-flowered kerria selection produces the same bright green, arching, bamboo-like canes as the species but with fully double, pompom-shaped, golden-yellow flowers in mid-spring that resemble small ranunculus blooms and last longer than the single form. It tolerates considerably more shade than most flowering shrubs while still blooming reliably, making it a good choice for a woodland edge, foundation planting, or naturalized shrub border, and its green stems provide subtle winter interest after leaf drop. Prune out a portion of the oldest canes at ground level right after flowering each year to keep the colony vigorous and well-shaped.

Abelia mosanensis is a deciduous Korean species grown chiefly for its intensely fragrant, pink-budded, white to pale pink tubular flowers borne in dense clusters in late spring, filling the garden with a sweet scent often compared to lilac or daphne, followed by attractive burgundy-red fall foliage color. Unlike the more commonly planted evergreen glossy abelia (Abelia x grandiflora), this species drops its leaves in winter and blooms in one strong spring flush rather than repeating through summer, making it a specialty fragrance shrub rather than a long-season landscape workhorse. Site it near a patio, walkway, or window where its brief but powerful spring fragrance can be fully appreciated, and prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape.

Rhodotypos scandens is a tough, adaptable, deciduous shrub related to Kerria, with pleated, sharply toothed, opposite leaves and single, four-petaled white flowers in mid-spring followed by clusters of glossy, jet-black, pea-sized fruit that persist into winter and give the plant its common name. It is one of the most shade-tolerant flowering shrubs available, thriving in the deep, dry shade beneath mature trees where few other shrubs perform, and asks for essentially no maintenance once established beyond occasional renewal pruning. Because it seeds itself freely and can naturalize into nearby wooded areas in some regions, it is best used in a contained landscape bed rather than adjacent to natural woodland, with faded flowers removed before seed matures if spread is a concern.

Michelia yunnanensis (sometimes sold as Magnolia laevifolia) is a dense, compact, evergreen relative of magnolia from southwestern China, with small, glossy, deep green leaves backed in rusty brown felt and creamy white, cup-shaped, intensely fragrant flowers with a fruity, banana-like scent opening from furry brown buds in spring. Its naturally tidy, rounded habit needs little pruning to stay attractive, making it a low-maintenance evergreen specimen or informal hedge for a shaded courtyard or foundation planting in warm-climate gardens. It appreciates consistent moisture and acidic soil similar to camellia and azalea, and benefits from a wind-sheltered site at the cooler edge of its hardiness range.
